# Mia: full guides

> Pregnancy, birth and after-birth guides from Mia (https://miapregnancy.com). Education, not medical advice. Always contact a midwife or doctor for concerns.

# Pregnancy week by week
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/pregnancy-week-by-week/
Stage: Pregnancy

Each week brings small changes for you and your baby. Mia gives you one clear view of your week: how big your baby is, what your body is doing and one thing worth doing now.

## In short
- Weeks 1 to 13: The first trimester. Tiredness and nausea are common. Your first scan is usually around week 12.
- Weeks 14 to 27: The second trimester. Many people feel more energy. You may feel the first movements.
- Weeks 28 to 40: The third trimester. Baby grows fast. From week 24, notice your baby’s usual pattern of movements.
- After 40 weeks: Many babies arrive after their due date. Your midwife will talk with you about your options.

## How pregnancy weeks are counted
Pregnancy is counted from the first day of your last period, not from the day you conceived. That is why you are already “four weeks pregnant” when a test first turns positive. A full-term pregnancy is around 40 weeks, and anywhere from 37 to 42 weeks is normal.
Your due date is a best guess. Only about one baby in twenty arrives on the exact day. Your dating scan, usually between weeks 10 and 14, gives the most reliable date.

## The first trimester: weeks 1 to 13
Your baby’s heart, brain and spine begin to form in these weeks. By week 12 your baby is fully formed and about the size of a plum, though still very small.
For many people this is the hardest stretch. Tiredness, nausea, sore breasts and big feelings are common, even though nobody can see your bump yet. Rest when you can and keep meals small and simple.

## The second trimester: weeks 14 to 27
Energy often comes back and nausea fades. Your bump starts to show, and somewhere between weeks 16 and 24 you will likely feel the first flutters of movement.
The anomaly scan, offered at 18 to 21 weeks, checks how your baby is growing. This is also a good time to start thinking about where you want to give birth and to book antenatal classes.

## The third trimester: weeks 28 to 40
Your baby grows quickly, puts on fat and usually turns head down. You may feel heavier, more breathless and more tired again. Sleeping on your side from week 28 is advised.
From now on, get to know your baby’s usual pattern of movements. Pack your bag around week 36, finish your birth plan and talk with your midwife about the signs of labour.

## Your check-ups
In the UK, a first pregnancy usually has around ten antenatal appointments, and later pregnancies around seven. Your midwife checks your blood pressure, urine and the growth of your bump, and talks you through tests and choices.
Bring your questions. Writing them down between visits helps. No question is too small.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby moves less than usual, or the pattern changes
- You have bleeding from your vagina
- Fluid leaks from your vagina
- You have a bad headache, problems with your eyes, or sudden swelling of your face, hands or feet
- You have strong tummy pain that does not go away
- You have itching, especially on your hands and feet, later in pregnancy

## Questions
Q: When should I call my midwife?
A: If your baby moves less than usual, if you bleed, or if something feels wrong. Do not wait for your next visit.
Q: Does Mia replace my check-ups?
A: No. Mia helps you understand your week. Your midwife and doctor look after you.
Q: How is my due date worked out?
A: It is counted as 40 weeks from the first day of your last period, then usually adjusted at your dating scan.
Q: How many scans will I have?
A: Most people in the UK are offered two: a dating scan at 10 to 14 weeks and an anomaly scan at 18 to 21 weeks. You may be offered more if needed.
Q: Is it normal not to feel pregnant?
A: Yes. Symptoms come and go, and some people have very few. If you are worried, talk to your midwife.

Evidence: Based on NHS pregnancy guidance and WHO antenatal care recommendations.
Sources: NHS: Your pregnancy and baby guide; NICE guideline NG201: Antenatal care; WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience

---

# First trimester: what to expect
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/first-trimester/
Stage: Pregnancy

The first trimester can feel big and quiet at the same time. Here is what is common, what helps, and when to call someone.

## In short
- Common symptoms: Tiredness, nausea, tender breasts and needing to pee more are very common.
- Nausea: Small, regular snacks and sips of water can help. If you cannot keep anything down, call your midwife or doctor.
- Your first scan: The dating scan is usually offered around weeks 10 to 14.
- Call if: You have heavy bleeding, strong one-sided pain or feel very unwell. Get help the same day.

## What is happening in your body
Pregnancy hormones rise fast in the first weeks. They support your baby but can leave you tired, sick, emotional and needing to pee more. Your breasts may feel full and tender.
Your baby goes from a tiny cluster of cells to a fully formed baby by week 12. The heart starts beating at around six weeks.

## Nausea and sickness
Up to eight in ten pregnant people have nausea, often called morning sickness, though it can happen at any time of day. It usually eases by weeks 16 to 20.
Small, frequent snacks, plain foods, sips of water and rest can help. Ginger helps some people. If you cannot keep food or drink down, or you feel faint, you may have a more serious form called hyperemesis gravidarum. Call your midwife or GP, as treatment is available.

## Tiredness and mood
Feeling exhausted is very common and is not a sign that anything is wrong. Go to bed early, say yes to help and lower the bar on everything else for a while.
Mood swings, worry and low days are common too. If you feel low most of the time, or anxious in a way that stops you living your life, tell your midwife. Mental health support is part of pregnancy care.

## Your first appointments
Your booking appointment with a midwife usually happens by week 10. You will talk about your health, your history and your choices, and be offered blood tests.
The dating scan is offered between weeks 10 and 14. It checks your baby’s heartbeat, confirms your due date and can be combined with screening tests if you choose them.

## Looking after yourself now
Take folic acid until week 12 and vitamin D throughout pregnancy, as advised in the UK. Avoid alcohol and smoking, and check any medicines with a pharmacist or doctor.
Gentle movement such as walking or swimming is good if you feel up to it. If you were active before, you can usually carry on with some changes.

## When to call your midwife
- Heavy bleeding, or bleeding with pain
- Strong pain on one side of your tummy, or pain in the tip of your shoulder
- You cannot keep food or fluids down for 24 hours
- You feel faint or very unwell
- Pain or burning when you pee, or a high temperature

## Questions
Q: What should I take in early pregnancy?
A: In the UK, 400 micrograms of folic acid daily is advised before pregnancy and until week 12. Ask your midwife what suits you.
Q: Is spotting normal?
A: Light spotting can be common but always tell your midwife. Call at once if bleeding is heavy or with pain.
Q: When should I tell people?
A: That is up to you. Many people wait until after the 12-week scan, but some share earlier for support.
Q: Is cramping normal?
A: Mild, period-like cramping can be common early on. Strong or one-sided pain, or pain with bleeding, needs a call the same day.
Q: Can I drink coffee?
A: Yes, but keep caffeine under 200 mg a day, about two mugs of instant coffee.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on the first trimester and NICE antenatal care guidance.
Sources: NHS: Weeks 1 to 12; NHS: Vomiting and morning sickness in pregnancy; NICE guideline NG201: Antenatal care

---

# Second trimester: weeks 14 to 27
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/second-trimester/
Stage: Pregnancy

Many people feel their best in the second trimester. Mia explains the changes, the scan and what to watch for.

## In short
- More energy: Nausea often eases and energy returns for many people.
- The anomaly scan: Usually offered at 18 to 21 weeks. It checks how baby is growing.
- First movements: You may feel flutters from around 16 to 24 weeks.
- Common aches: Back, hip and round ligament pain are common. Gentle movement and rest can help.

## Feeling more like yourself
For many people, weeks 14 to 27 feel easier. Nausea and tiredness often fade, and your energy comes back. It can be a good time to plan, travel or start antenatal classes.
Your bump begins to show, and your body keeps changing. Skin may darken in places and stretch marks can appear. Both are common and often fade after birth.

## Your baby is growing
Your baby grows from about 8 cm to around 35 cm long in these weeks. They can hear sounds, suck their thumb and move a lot, even before you feel it.
Most people feel the first movements between weeks 16 and 24. At first they feel like flutters or bubbles. In a first pregnancy you may notice them later.

## The anomaly scan
The mid-pregnancy scan, offered at 18 to 21 weeks, looks closely at your baby’s body, organs and growth. It also checks where the placenta is.
You can usually ask to find out the sex at this scan if the hospital offers it. Bring someone with you if you would like support.

## Common aches and how to ease them
Back pain, round ligament pain (a sharp pull low on the sides of the bump), heartburn and leg cramps are common. Good posture, gentle stretching, warm baths and smaller meals can help.
Pelvic girdle pain, felt at the front or back of the pelvis, is common too. It is not harmful to your baby, but tell your midwife. A physiotherapist can help a lot.

## Good things to do now
Keep moving most days. Start pelvic floor exercises if you have not already. Book antenatal classes, and start thinking about where you want to give birth.
From week 28 you will go to sleep on your side, so this is a good time to find a comfortable pillow set-up.

## When to call your midwife
- Bleeding or fluid leaking from your vagina
- Regular tightenings or period-like pain before 37 weeks
- Once you know their pattern: your baby moves less than usual
- A bad headache, blurred vision or sudden swelling
- Pain or burning when you pee, or a fever

## Questions
Q: Can I travel in the second trimester?
A: Often yes, and many find it the easiest time. Check with your midwife first.
Q: Should I sleep on my side?
A: From the third trimester, going to sleep on your side is advised. Do not worry if you wake on your back.
Q: When will I feel my baby kick?
A: Usually between weeks 16 and 24. It may be later in a first pregnancy.
Q: Is it safe to travel?
A: Often yes, and many find this the easiest time. Check with your midwife and your travel insurance.
Q: Can I have sex?
A: Yes, for most people. Your midwife will tell you if there is a reason not to.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on the second trimester and the NHS fetal anomaly screening programme.
Sources: NHS: Weeks 13 to 27; NHS fetal anomaly screening programme; NHS: Pelvic pain in pregnancy

---

# Third trimester: weeks 28 to 40
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/third-trimester/
Stage: Pregnancy

The last stretch brings big changes. Mia helps you get ready and know when to call.

## In short
- Baby grows fast: Baby puts on weight and gets into position for birth, often head down.
- Know the movements: Learn your baby’s usual pattern and call the same day if it changes.
- Get ready: Finish your birth plan, pack your bag and plan the journey to your birth place.
- Call if: You have bleeding, severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling or itching on your hands and feet.

## Your baby in the last weeks
From week 28 your baby gains weight quickly, builds fat and gets ready to breathe and feed. Most babies settle head down by week 36.
Babies keep moving right up to and during labour. Movements may feel different as space gets tight, more rolls and pushes than kicks, but they should not slow down.

## How your body feels
You may feel heavier, short of breath, and need to pee often. Heartburn, swollen ankles, back ache and poor sleep are all common.
Rest with your feet up, eat smaller meals and sleep on your side with a pillow between your knees. Ask for help with lifting and long days.

## Why side sleeping matters
Research has linked going to sleep on your back after 28 weeks with a higher risk of stillbirth. Going to sleep on your side, either side, is safer.
If you wake up on your back, do not worry. Just turn onto your side and go back to sleep.

## Getting ready for birth
Finish your birth plan and talk it through with your midwife. Pack your hospital bag by week 36, and plan how you will get to your birth place.
Learn the signs of labour, and know who to call and when. Practise your breathing and positions so they feel familiar.

## If your baby is late
Many first babies arrive after their due date. Your midwife may offer a membrane sweep from around 39 to 41 weeks.
If labour has not started by around 41 weeks, you will be offered induction. You can also choose to wait with extra monitoring. Ask about the risks and benefits of each.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby moves less than usual, or the pattern changes. Call the same day
- Bleeding from your vagina
- Your waters break, or fluid leaks
- A bad headache, vision changes, or sudden swelling of your face, hands or feet
- Itching, especially on your hands and feet
- Regular contractions before 37 weeks

## Questions
Q: Is it normal to feel more tired?
A: Yes. Rest when you can and accept help.
Q: Why is sleeping on my side advised?
A: Research links going to sleep on the back in late pregnancy with a higher risk of stillbirth. Side sleeping is safer.
Q: What if my baby is breech?
A: Your midwife may offer a procedure to turn baby (ECV) around 36 to 37 weeks, or talk about a planned caesarean or vaginal breech birth.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE antenatal care guidance.
Sources: NHS: Weeks 28 to 40; Tommy’s: Sleep on side campaign; NICE guideline NG207: Inducing labour

---

# Baby movements in pregnancy
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/baby-movements/
Stage: Pregnancy

Your baby’s movements tell you they are doing well. Learn their usual pattern, and what to do if it changes.

## In short
- When you feel them: Many people feel the first movements between weeks 16 and 24. It may be later in a first pregnancy.
- Know your baby’s pattern: There is no set number of kicks. Get to know what is usual for your baby.
- Less movement: If your baby moves less than usual, call your midwife or maternity unit the same day. Do not wait until the next day.
- Do not use apps to reassure you: Do not rely on a home doppler or an app to check on baby. Always call your midwife.

## Why movements matter
If your baby is not well, they may be less active than usual. Less movement can be a sign of a problem, and the sooner it is found the better.
Feeling your baby move is a reassurance that they are well. A reduction or a change in the pattern is what matters.

## When you will feel them
Most people feel their baby move between 16 and 24 weeks. If this is your first baby, you might not feel movements until after 20 weeks.
Movements can feel like a gentle swirling or fluttering, then kicks, swishes, rolls and jerks as your baby grows.
If you have not felt your baby move by 24 weeks, tell your midwife. They will check your baby’s heartbeat and movements.

## What is normal
There is no set number of movements. Every baby is different, and you do not need to count kicks. What matters is getting to know your own baby’s usual pattern from day to day.
Afternoon and evening are often the busiest times. Your baby also has sleep periods, mostly 20 to 40 minutes and rarely longer than 90 minutes, when they usually do not move.
The number of movements tends to go up until about 32 weeks, then stays about the same. You should feel your baby move right up to and during labour.

## Why you may notice less
You are less likely to notice movements when you are busy or active. A placenta at the front of your womb can also make movements harder to feel.
Strong pain relief or sedatives, alcohol and smoking can make a baby move less. Sometimes a baby moves less because they are unwell.

## If movements change
Call your midwife or maternity unit straight away if your baby is moving less than usual, you cannot feel them any more, or the pattern changes. Do not wait until the next day, even in the middle of the night.
Never go to sleep ignoring a change in your baby’s movements. Call each time it happens, even if everything was fine before.
Do not use a home doppler or heartbeat kit. It is not a reliable way to check on your baby, and hearing a heartbeat does not mean your baby is well.
There is not enough evidence to recommend a movement chart as routine. Knowing your baby’s own pattern matters more.

## What care to expect
After 28 weeks you must contact your midwife or maternity unit immediately. You will be asked about the movements and checked, and your baby’s heartbeat will be listened to.
Between 24 and 28 weeks, call your midwife or unit. They will check your baby’s heartbeat and give you a full check-up. A scan may be arranged.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby is moving less than usual
- The pattern of movements changes
- You cannot feel your baby move any more. Call straight away
- You have not felt your baby move by week 24

## Questions
Q: Should I try a cold drink or a snack to wake my baby?
A: Do not wait or rely on tricks at home. If movements are reduced or changed, call your midwife or maternity unit straight away.
Q: Do babies move less near the end?
A: No. Babies keep moving up to and during labour.
Q: Do I need to count kicks?
A: No. There is no set number. Get to know your baby’s usual pattern and call if it changes or slows down.
Q: Do babies move less near the end of pregnancy?
A: No. The number of movements tends to stay about the same after 32 weeks, and you should feel your baby right up to and during labour.
Q: What if I called before and everything was fine?
A: Call again each time. Midwives would rather check than have you wait.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on baby movements and Tommy’s and RCOG advice on reduced movements.
Sources: Your baby’s movements (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/your-babys-movements/); Your baby’s movements in pregnancy (https://www.rcog.org.uk/for-the-public/browse-our-patient-information/your-babys-movements-in-pregnancy/)

# What to eat in pregnancy and foods to avoid
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/pregnancy-nutrition/
Stage: Pregnancy

You do not need to eat for two. Mia explains what helps you and your baby, and which foods to avoid, without the stress.

## In short
- Eat a varied diet: Fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, protein and dairy or alternatives. You need only a little extra energy in the last trimester.
- Key supplements: In the UK, folic acid until week 12 and vitamin D all pregnancy are advised. Ask your midwife what suits you.
- Foods to avoid: Avoid raw or undercooked eggs not marked Lion, unpasteurised soft cheeses, pâté, liver and raw or undercooked meat. Limit some fish.
- Caffeine and alcohol: Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day, about two mugs of instant coffee. The safest choice with alcohol is none.

## Eating well, without stress
You do not need a special diet. Aim for a mix of fruit and vegetables, wholegrains, protein such as beans, eggs, fish or meat, and dairy or fortified alternatives.
You only need about 200 extra calories a day in the last three months, roughly a slice of toast with peanut butter. Eating for two is a myth.

## Supplements in the UK
Take 400 micrograms of folic acid daily before pregnancy and until week 12. It helps prevent problems with the baby’s spine. Some people need a higher dose, so ask your GP.
Take 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding. Avoid supplements with vitamin A (retinol), as too much can harm your baby.

## Foods to avoid
Avoid unpasteurised milk and soft cheeses with a white rind (such as brie) unless cooked until steaming. Avoid all pâté, liver, and raw or undercooked meat.
British Lion eggs can be eaten runny. Other eggs should be cooked until firm. Wash fruit and vegetables well.

## Fish
Fish is good for you and your baby. Aim for two portions a week, including one of oily fish.
Have no more than two portions of oily fish, such as salmon or mackerel, a week. Avoid shark, swordfish and marlin, and limit tuna.

## Caffeine and alcohol
Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day. That is about two mugs of instant coffee or one mug of filter coffee. Tea, cola and chocolate count too.
The safest choice is no alcohol at all in pregnancy. If you drank before you knew you were pregnant, try not to worry, and talk to your midwife.

## When to call your midwife
- You cannot keep food or fluids down
- You are losing weight because of sickness
- You think you have eaten something unsafe and feel unwell, with fever or vomiting

## Questions
Q: Do I need to eat for two?
A: No. You need about 200 extra calories a day only in the last three months.
Q: Is it safe to eat fish?
A: Yes, and one or two portions a week is good. Avoid shark, swordfish and marlin, and limit oily fish.
Q: Can I eat peanuts?
A: Yes, unless you are allergic. There is no need to avoid them in pregnancy.
Q: Is a vegan diet safe in pregnancy?
A: Yes, with planning. You may need extra vitamin B12, iron, iodine and omega-3. Ask your midwife.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on foods to avoid and vitamins in pregnancy.
Sources: NHS: Foods to avoid in pregnancy; NHS: Vitamins, supplements and nutrition in pregnancy; NHS: Have a healthy diet in pregnancy

---

# Exercise in pregnancy: what is safe
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/exercise-in-pregnancy/
Stage: Pregnancy

Moving in pregnancy is good for you and your baby. Mia shows what is safe, what to avoid and when to stop.

## In short
- Keep moving: About 150 minutes of moderate activity a week is advised if you are well. Walking and swimming are easy places to start.
- Strength and stretching: Gentle strength work, yoga and pelvic floor exercises are fine for most people. Tell the teacher you are pregnant.
- What to avoid: Avoid contact sports, activities with a risk of falling, and lying flat on your back for long periods later on.
- Stop and call if: You feel dizzy, short of breath, have chest pain, bleeding, fluid leaking or less baby movement.

## Why moving helps
Regular activity in pregnancy is linked with better mood and sleep, less back pain, and a lower chance of high blood pressure and gestational diabetes.
It can also help you feel stronger for labour and recover faster after the birth.

## How much is enough
UK advice is about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as five 30-minute walks, plus some strength work twice a week.
Moderate means you can still talk but not sing. If you were not active before, start with 10 minutes a day and build up slowly.

## Good choices
Walking, swimming, aqua natal classes, stationary cycling, pregnancy yoga and Pilates are all good options.
Strength work with light weights or your body weight is fine for most people. Tell any teacher you are pregnant.

## What to avoid
Avoid contact sports such as kickboxing, and activities where you could fall, such as horse riding or skiing. Avoid scuba diving.
After about 16 weeks, avoid lying flat on your back for long periods during exercise, as it can make you feel faint.

## Your pelvic floor
Pelvic floor exercises help support your bladder and bowel, and can help prevent leaking. Try to do them every day in pregnancy and after birth.
Squeeze and lift as if stopping a wee, hold for a few seconds, then relax. Add quick squeezes too.

## When to call your midwife
- You feel dizzy or faint
- Chest pain, or shortness of breath before you start
- Bleeding or fluid leaking from your vagina
- Painful contractions
- Calf pain or swelling
- Your baby moves less than usual

## Questions
Q: Can I keep running?
A: Many people can if they were runners before. Listen to your body and talk to your midwife.
Q: Is exercise bad for the baby?
A: No. For most healthy pregnancies, regular activity is safe and linked with benefits.
Q: Can I do sit-ups?
A: Avoid hard ab work like crunches later on. Gentle core work and pelvic floor exercises are better.

Evidence: Based on NHS and UK Chief Medical Officers’ guidance on exercise in pregnancy.
Sources: UK Chief Medical Officers: Physical activity in pregnancy; NHS: Exercise in pregnancy; RCOG: Exercise in pregnancy

---

# Braxton Hicks contractions or real labour?
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/braxton-hicks/
Stage: Pregnancy

Practice tightenings can feel strong and worrying. Mia helps you tell them apart from true labour.

## In short
- What they feel like: A tightening across your belly that comes and goes, often irregular and not painful.
- What helps: Change position, rest, have a warm bath and drink water.
- Signs of labour: Contractions that get stronger, longer and closer together, and do not ease with rest.
- Call if: You have regular contractions before week 37, bleeding, fluid leaking, or reduced baby movement.

## What Braxton Hicks are
Braxton Hicks are tightenings of your womb that come and go. They are sometimes called practice contractions or false labour. They are one of the ways your body gets ready for birth.
Unlike labour contractions, they do not open your cervix, the entrance to your womb. So even when they feel strong, they are not a sign that labour has started.
Not everyone notices them, and that is fine too. If you do, it is most often in the second or third trimester.

## What they feel like
Many people describe a tightening across the bump, a bit like mild period cramps. Your bump may feel hard for a minute or two, then soften again.
They can be uncomfortable, but they are usually not painful. They do not last long, they do not come often and they do not build up.
Near your due date they can feel stronger or come more often. That is why it can be hard to tell them apart from the start of labour.

## What sets them off
Nobody knows exactly why they happen. Being very active, a full bladder, sex and not drinking enough can all bring them on.
Experts think they help tone the muscles of your womb, ready for labour.

## What helps
Change what you are doing. If you have been on your feet a lot, lie down. If you have been sitting for a long time, go for a gentle walk.
A warm bath, a nap, slow breathing and a glass of water can all help them settle.

## How real labour is different
Labour contractions come at regular times and get longer, stronger and closer together. They do not ease when you rest or change position.
Labour often starts slowly. This early part, called the latent phase, can take hours or even days, and you will usually be advised to stay at home for it.
Other signs that labour may be starting are a show (a plug of pink, sticky mucus coming away), backache, needing the toilet a lot, and your waters breaking.
Your midwife will usually suggest you call when contractions come about every 5 minutes or more often.

## If labour does start
At the start of labour your cervix softens and opens. This latent phase is usually the longest part and can take many hours, sometimes days.
During the day, stay upright and gently active. At night, rest and sleep if you can. Eat and drink, because you will need energy later.
Breathing, a back rub, a warm bath or shower and paracetamol (taken as the packet says) can ease early contractions.

## Before 37 weeks
Labour before 37 weeks is called premature labour. About 8 in 100 babies are born early.
If you are less than 37 weeks and have regular tightenings, period-type pains, unusual backache or a trickle of fluid, call your maternity unit. They can check whether labour is starting.

## When tummy pain is something else
Mild pain that goes away when you rest, change position or go to the toilet is usually nothing to worry about.
Pain that is strong, or does not go away after 30 to 60 minutes of rest, needs a call to your maternity unit straight away. The same goes for pain with bleeding, fluid leaking or pain when you pee.

## When to call your midwife
- You are not sure if it is Braxton Hicks or labour
- Regular tightenings before 37 weeks
- Bleeding from your vagina, or your waters break
- Contractions lasting longer than 2 minutes, or 6 or more in 10 minutes
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Strong tummy pain that does not ease after resting

## Questions
Q: When do they start?
A: Some people feel them from the second trimester. They are more common later.
Q: Can they hurt?
A: They can feel uncomfortable. Strong pain that does not ease needs a call to your midwife.
Q: How many Braxton Hicks a day is normal?
A: There is no set number. What matters is the pattern: they stay irregular and short and ease with rest. If they become regular, call your maternity unit. If you are under 37 weeks, call if they keep going.
Q: Can Braxton Hicks hurt my baby?
A: No. They are a normal part of pregnancy. Keep noticing your baby’s usual movements, and call if they slow down or change.
Q: I am not sure what I am feeling. Is it OK to call?
A: Yes. Midwives would rather check and reassure you than have you worry at home. Maternity units are open day and night.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on Braxton Hicks and signs of labour.
Sources: Signs that labour has begun (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/signs-that-labour-has-begun/); Braxton Hicks (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/braxton-hicks); The stages of labour and birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/the-stages-of-labour-and-birth/); Premature labour and birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/premature-labour-and-birth/); Stomach pain in pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/common-symptoms/stomach-pain/)

# Natural birth, explained honestly
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/natural-birth/
Stage: Birth

A natural birth is a labour that starts and carries on by itself, with only the medical help you need. Here is what tends to help, how strong the evidence is, and what your other options look like.

## In short
- Move and stay upright: Walking, swaying and kneeling in early labour can help labour move along. Research links upright positions with a shorter first stage.
- Continuous support: Having one person with you the whole time, like a doula or partner, is linked with fewer interventions and a better experience.
- Dim light and calm: A quiet, private room helps you feel safe. Feeling safe helps labour hormones do their work.
- Every option is fine: Pain relief, induction or a caesarean can be the right choice. Mia explains them too, without judgement.

## What natural birth means
Natural birth usually means labour that starts on its own and moves on with as little medical help as is safe for you and your baby. It often means birth without an epidural, using movement, water and support to cope.
It is not a test you pass or fail. Many births include some help along the way, and that is still your birth.

## Why your hormones matter
Labour is driven by hormones, mainly oxytocin. Oxytocin works best when you feel safe, warm, private and unhurried. Fear and stress hormones can slow labour down.
That is why dim light, quiet voices, a familiar person and freedom to move can make a real difference.

## Move and stay upright
Walking, swaying, kneeling and leaning forward use gravity and help your baby move down. A Cochrane review found upright positions in the first stage are linked with a shorter labour and fewer epidurals.
A birth ball, a pool or a partner to lean on all help. Change position whenever your body asks.

## Continuous support
Having one person with you the whole way through, such as a partner, friend or doula, is one of the best-proven ways to help labour. It is linked with fewer interventions and a better birth experience.
Talk with your support person before labour about what helps you and what you want.

## Getting ready in pregnancy
Antenatal classes, breathing practice and learning the stages of labour all help you feel calm and ready.
Write down your wishes, and talk them through with your midwife. Think about where you want to give birth, since midwife-led units and home births have fewer interventions for people with healthy pregnancies.

## Every option is fine
Pain relief, induction or a caesarean can be the right choice for you or your baby. Mia explains these fairly too.
If plans change, you can still keep things that matter to you, like skin-to-skin, dim lights or your music.

## When to call your midwife
- Your waters break, especially if the fluid is green, brown or smells
- You have bleeding
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Contractions are regular and strong, or you feel you need support
- You feel unsure or worried. Calling is always fine

## Questions
Q: Is natural birth safer?
A: It depends on your health and your pregnancy. Talk it through with your midwife.
Q: Can I change my mind in labour?
A: Yes. Your birth plan is a wish list, not a contract.
Q: Does natural birth hurt more?
A: Labour is intense for most people. Movement, water, breathing and support can help a lot, and pain relief is always there if you want it.

Evidence: Based on Cochrane reviews of upright positions in labour and of continuous support in labour.
Sources: Cochrane review: Maternal positions and mobility during first stage labour; Cochrane review: Continuous support for women during childbirth; NICE guideline NG235: Intrapartum care

---

# Signs of labour: when to call your midwife
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/signs-of-labour/
Stage: Birth

Labour often starts slowly. Here are the early signs, what real contractions feel like and when to call your midwife, so you are never guessing alone.

## In short
- Early signs: Regular tightenings, a show (a pink or bloody mucus plug), backache or a watery trickle can all be early signs.
- Real or practice?: Practice contractions (Braxton Hicks) are irregular and ease with rest. Real contractions get longer, stronger and closer together.
- When to call: Call your midwife or maternity unit if your waters break, if you bleed, if baby moves less, or if contractions are regular and strong.
- At home first: Many people stay at home in early labour: eat lightly, drink, rest and move. Your midwife will guide you on when to come in.

## The signs
Labour may be starting if you have contractions or tightenings, a “show”, backache, an urge to go to the toilet, or your waters break.
An urge to go to the toilet comes from your baby’s head pressing on your bowel.

## Contractions
In a contraction your womb tightens, then relaxes. For some people it feels like extreme period pain. Put your hand on your bump and you will feel it get hard, then ease.
Labour contractions get longer, stronger and more frequent as labour goes on. Practice contractions (Braxton Hicks) are usually painless, short, infrequent and do not build up.

## A show
During pregnancy a plug of mucus sits in your cervix. It comes away just before or in early labour. It is sticky, jelly-like and pink because it holds a little blood.
It may come in one blob or in pieces. Labour may follow quickly or take a few days, and some people have no show. If you lose more blood than that, call your midwife or hospital straight away.

## Your waters breaking
Your waters will most likely break during labour, but they can break before it starts. You may feel a slow trickle or a sudden gush.
Amniotic fluid is clear and pale. Use a period pad, not a tampon, so your midwife can check the colour. Tell your midwife straight away if the fluid is smelly or coloured, or if you are losing blood.
Most people go into labour within 24 hours of their waters breaking. If you do not, you will be offered an induction because there is a small increased risk of infection.

## The early stage
The start of labour is called the latent phase. Your cervix softens and thins, and starts to open. It can take hours, or sometimes days, and you will probably be advised to stay at home.
Stay upright and gently active in the day, and rest at night if you can. Eat and drink. Breathing, massage, a warm bath or shower and paracetamol can help.
Labour is called established when your cervix is about 4 cm open and contractions are stronger and more regular.

## When to call
Call your midwife or maternity unit if you think you are in labour, or if contractions come every 5 minutes or more often. You can also call if you are unsure or worried about anything.
Call urgently if your waters break, you have vaginal bleeding, your baby moves less, you are under 37 weeks, a contraction lasts longer than 2 minutes, or you have 6 or more contractions in 10 minutes. Do not wait until morning.
Call 999 if you think your baby is coming now and you have a strong urge to push. If you cannot reach your midwife or unit, call 111.

## When to call your midwife
- Contractions every 5 minutes or closer
- Your waters break
- Bleeding from your vagina
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Under 37 weeks and you think you are in labour
- A contraction lasts over 2 minutes, or 6 or more in 10 minutes

## Questions
Q: What if my waters break?
A: Call your midwife or maternity unit. Note the time and the colour of the fluid.
Q: How far apart are contractions when I should go in?
A: Your midwife will tell you what suits you. Many units advise calling when they come regularly every 5 minutes or sooner.
Q: How will I know it is real labour?
A: Real contractions get longer, stronger and closer together, and do not ease when you rest or change position. If you are unsure, call your midwife or maternity unit.
Q: Should I go to hospital straight away?
A: Not usually. In early labour you will probably be advised to stay at home. Call first and they will tell you when to come in.
Q: What if my waters break but there are no contractions?
A: Call your midwife. Most people go into labour within 24 hours. If you do not, you will be offered an induction.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on signs of labour and NICE intrapartum care guidance.
Sources: Signs that labour has begun (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/signs-that-labour-has-begun/); The stages of labour and birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/the-stages-of-labour-and-birth/)

---

# Best positions for labour and birth
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/labour-positions/
Stage: Birth

How you move in labour can make a real difference. Here are simple positions to try, and why they help.

## In short
- Stay upright: Standing, walking and leaning on a partner use gravity and can help baby move down.
- Use a birth ball: Sitting and rocking on a ball can ease backache and keep your hips loose.
- Hands and knees: This takes weight off your back and can help if baby is lying back to back.
- Change often: Try a new position every 30 minutes or so. Your body will tell you what feels right.

## Why position matters
In labour, your baby turns and moves down through your pelvis. Being upright and changing position gives your pelvis room and lets gravity help.
Research shows upright positions in the first stage are linked with a shorter labour, fewer epidurals and fewer caesareans.

## Positions for early labour
Walk, sway your hips, or lean forward on a counter or your partner. Rock or circle your hips on a birth ball.
Rest between contractions, and lie on your side when you need a break.

## Positions for back pain
Kneeling on all fours, or leaning forward over a ball or bed, takes pressure off your back. It can help if your baby is lying back to back.
Ask your partner to press firmly on your lower back during contractions.

## Positions for pushing
Kneeling, squatting, standing, or lying on your side can all work for pushing. Side-lying can be gentle on your perineum.
Lying on your back is common but not always needed. Ask your midwife to help you find what feels right.

## With monitoring or an epidural
Many units have wireless monitors so you can still move. With an epidural, you can still change position in bed, sit up, lie on your side or use a peanut ball between your knees.

## When to call your midwife
- Your waters break
- Bleeding
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Contractions are strong and regular

## Questions
Q: Can I move with a monitor or drip?
A: Often, yes. Ask your midwife which positions work with your equipment.
Q: Is lying on my back bad?
A: It is not unsafe for everyone, but upright and side positions are linked with a shorter first stage.
Q: Should I practise positions?
A: Yes. Trying them in late pregnancy makes them easier to use in labour.

Evidence: Based on the Cochrane review of positions in the first stage of labour and NICE intrapartum care guidance.
Sources: Cochrane review: Maternal positions and mobility during first stage labour; NICE guideline NG235: Intrapartum care

---

# Labour and birth in water
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/water-birth/
Stage: Birth

Warm water can help you relax and move freely in labour, and many birth centres and hospitals have a pool. Here is what the research found, and how to ask for one.

## In short
- Why water helps: Warm water supports your weight and can ease pain. Some people need less other pain relief.
- What the research found: The large UK POOL study looked at tens of thousands of births. For women with low-risk pregnancies, birth in water was not linked with more harm to babies.
- Who it suits: Usually people with a healthy, low-risk pregnancy. Your midwife will tell you if it suits you.
- Plan ahead: Ask early if your birth place has a pool, and what happens if it is in use.

## Why water helps
Warm water supports your weight, helps you relax and lets you move freely. Many people find it eases pain.
Using a pool in labour is linked with less need for an epidural. Some people labour in the pool and get out to give birth.

## What the research found
The UK POOL study looked at tens of thousands of births. For women with healthy, low-risk pregnancies, giving birth in water was not linked with more harm to babies.
It also did not find more serious tears for women who gave birth in water.

## Who it suits
Water birth usually suits people with a healthy, low-risk pregnancy at term. Your midwife will tell you if it suits you.
It may not be advised if you have certain health conditions, need continuous monitoring, or have had certain drugs for pain.

## How to plan for a pool
Ask early whether your birth place has pools and what happens if they are in use. Some people hire a pool for a home birth.
Your midwife will keep an eye on the water temperature and on your baby’s heartbeat with a waterproof device.

## When to call your midwife
- Your waters break
- Bleeding
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Contractions are strong and regular

## Questions
Q: Can I have pain relief in the pool?
A: Gas and air, yes. For an epidural you leave the pool.
Q: Do I have to give birth in the water?
A: No. Many people labour in the pool and give birth outside it.
Q: When can I get in?
A: Usually once labour is well established. Getting in too early may slow things down for some people.

Evidence: Based on the POOL cohort study (UK) and NHS guidance on water birth.
Sources: POOL study (UK, 2023) on waterbirth safety; NHS: Where to give birth; NICE guideline NG235: Intrapartum care

---

# What a doula does
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/doula/
Stage: Birth

A doula is a trained birth companion. They do not give medical care. They stay with you, help you feel steady and help you speak up for what you want.

## In short
- Before birth: Talks through your wishes, your fears and your birth plan with you.
- In labour: Stays with you the whole time. Helps with positions, breathing, touch and calm.
- After birth: Some doulas visit in the first weeks to help with feeding and rest.
- What the research found: Continuous support in labour is linked with more spontaneous births and a better experience of birth.

## What a doula does
A doula is a trained birth companion. They give emotional and practical support in pregnancy, in labour and often in the early weeks after birth.
A doula is not a midwife and does not do medical tasks. They stay with you, help you cope and help you feel heard.

## What the research says
A large Cochrane review found that continuous support in labour, especially from someone who is not a hospital staff member, is linked with more births without instruments or surgery, shorter labours and less need for pain relief.
People who had continuous support were also more likely to feel good about their birth.

## How a doula helps in labour
Massage, positions, breathing, reminding you of your wishes and calm words. They also support your partner, so they can rest and stay close.

## Finding and paying for a doula
Most doulas in the UK are private and paid. Some charities and volunteer schemes offer free or low-cost doulas.
Meet a few, and choose someone you feel relaxed with. Ask about their training, experience and backup plans.

## When to call your midwife
- A doula supports you, but your midwife is the person to call for any medical worry

## Questions
Q: Is a doula a midwife?
A: No. A midwife gives medical care. A doula gives emotional and practical support.
Q: Can my partner do this?
A: Yes, partly. Many people have both a partner and a doula.
Q: Can I have a doula and a partner?
A: Yes. A doula supports both of you.
Q: Will my hospital allow a doula?
A: Most do. Check your unit’s birth partner rules.
Q: Do doulas help with caesareans?
A: Many do, and can support you before and after.

Evidence: Based on the Cochrane review of continuous support for women during childbirth.
Sources: Cochrane review: Continuous support for women during childbirth; Doula UK

---

# Birth partner guide: how to support labour
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/birth-partner/
Stage: Birth

A birth partner can make a big difference. Mia gives partners a calm guide to what to do and what to say.

## In short
- Know the plan: Read the birth plan together. You can speak up for the wishes when your partner is busy coping.
- Comfort measures: Offer water, massage, a cool cloth, a change of position and calm words.
- Stay calm: Slow breathing from you helps. It is fine to ask the midwife to explain what is happening.
- Look after yourself: Eat, drink and take short breaks. You will be needed after the birth too.

## Your role
Your job is to help the person in labour feel safe, calm and heard. You do not need to know everything. Being there and staying calm matters most.

## Before labour
Read the birth plan together, so you know what matters to them. Learn the signs of labour and know who to call.
Pack your own bag, with snacks, a charger, a change of clothes and money for parking.

## In early labour
Time contractions, offer food and drinks, and encourage rest. Keep things calm and low-key at home.

## In active labour
Offer water between contractions, a cool cloth, massage or firm pressure on the lower back. Help with position changes.
Speak softly and keep the room calm. Ask the midwife questions if you are not sure what is happening.

## Speaking up
If something is offered, help your partner ask: what are the benefits, the risks, the alternatives, and what if we wait?
Be polite and calm. You are there to help them choose, not to choose for them.

## After the birth
Skin-to-skin is not just for the birthing parent. You can hold the baby too. Take photos if wanted, and help with the first feed.

## When to call your midwife
- The person in labour feels something is wrong
- Waters break, or there is bleeding
- Baby moves less than usual

## Questions
Q: What if I feel faint at the birth?
A: Sit down and tell the midwife. It is common and nothing to be embarrassed about.
Q: Should I speak up for my partner?
A: Yes, politely, about wishes you have talked through. Ask questions rather than argue.
Q: What should I bring?
A: Snacks, a charger, a change of clothes and money for parking.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance for birth partners and Cochrane evidence on continuous support in labour.
Sources: NHS: Tips for birth partners; Cochrane review: Continuous support for women during childbirth

---

# Breathing and calm for labour
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/hypnobirthing-breathing/
Stage: Birth

Slow, steady breathing can help you cope with contractions. These are simple techniques you can practise at home in a few minutes a day.

## In short
- Slow breathing: Breathe in through your nose, then out slowly through your mouth, longer than the in-breath.
- Relaxation: Soften your jaw, shoulders and hands. A relaxed body often means a calmer mind.
- Practise often: A few minutes a day in pregnancy makes it easier to use when labour comes.
- The evidence: Studies suggest relaxation-based preparation can reduce fear of birth. It does not replace pain relief if you want it.

## Why breathing helps
Slow breathing calms your nervous system. It helps you stay on top of each contraction instead of tensing against it.

## A simple technique
Breathe in through your nose for a count of four. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of six to eight. Let your shoulders drop as you breathe out.
In pushing, many people find a long, steady out-breath helpful, or follow their body’s urge.

## What hypnobirthing is
Hypnobirthing is a type of antenatal course using breathing, relaxation, visualisation and positive words. Many people find it helps them feel calmer and more in control.

## What the research says
Studies suggest relaxation-based preparation can reduce fear of birth and help people feel more satisfied. A UK trial did not find it reduced epidural use.
So it may help how you feel, even if it does not change medical outcomes.

## How to practise
Practise a few minutes a day from around week 28. Try it during Braxton Hicks, in the bath, or before sleep. Your partner can learn it too.

## When to call your midwife
- Breathing is a coping tool. For any worry, call your midwife

## Questions
Q: Is hypnobirthing the same as no pain?
A: No. It helps with fear and tension. Pain relief is still your choice.
Q: When should I start practising?
A: Many people start around week 28, but any time helps.
Q: Can it help with a caesarean?
A: Yes, many people use breathing and relaxation to stay calm.

Evidence: Based on Cochrane reviews of relaxation and antenatal education, and NHS guidance on coping with labour.
Sources: Cochrane review: Relaxation techniques for pain management in labour; SHIP trial (UK): self-hypnosis for intrapartum pain

---

# How to write a birth plan
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/birth-plan/
Stage: Birth

A birth plan is a short note about what matters to you in labour. Keep it to one page that your team can read in a minute.

## In short
- Keep it short: One page is enough. Use plain words and put your most important wishes first.
- What to include: Who you want with you, positions and movement, pain relief wishes, and your feeding plan.
- Plan for change: Birth can go a different way. Add what you would want if plans change, such as skin-to-skin after a caesarean.
- Share it early: Talk it through with your midwife before labour and bring a copy.

## What a birth plan is
A birth plan is a short note of what matters to you in labour and after the birth. It helps your team get to know you quickly.

## What to include
Who you want with you. Where you want to give birth. How you want to cope: movement, water, breathing or pain relief.
What happens after: skin-to-skin, delayed cord clamping, how you want to feed, and vitamin K for your baby.

## Plan for changes
Add a short section for if plans change, for example if you need induction, an assisted birth or a caesarean. What would still matter to you?

## How to write it
Keep it to one page. Use bullet points, and put the most important things first.
Talk it through with your midwife around weeks 34 to 36, and bring copies to your birth place.

## When to call your midwife
- If you are unsure about any part of your plan, ask your midwife at your next check-up

## Questions
Q: Is a birth plan a promise?
A: No. It is a wish list. Your team will keep you and your baby safe first.
Q: Who should see my birth plan?
A: Your midwife, your birth partner and anyone supporting you in labour.
Q: When should I write it?
A: Many people start around week 32 and finish by week 36.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE guidance on shared decision making in maternity care.
Sources: NHS: How to make a birth plan; NICE guideline NG235: Intrapartum care

# Home, birth centre or hospital: where to give birth
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/home-birth-or-hospital/
Stage: Birth

You have a choice about where to give birth. Mia explains each place fairly, so you can decide with your midwife.

## In short
- At home: With a midwife present. For healthy, low-risk pregnancies it is a safe option. Transfer to hospital is possible if needed.
- Midwife-led unit: A homelike setting with midwives. Medical help is nearby or on site.
- Hospital: Best if you or baby need extra care. Doctors and pain relief such as epidural are available.
- Ask your midwife: Your history matters. Ask what is safest and what is available near you.

## Your choice
In the UK you can choose where to give birth: at home, in a midwife-led unit, or in a hospital labour ward. Your choice may depend on your health and pregnancy.

## Home birth
Two midwives come to your home. For people with healthy, low-risk pregnancies who have had a baby before, it is as safe for babies as a hospital birth, with fewer interventions.
For first babies, home birth carries a small extra risk for the baby, and about four in ten first-time mothers transfer to hospital, usually for slow labour, not emergencies.

## Midwife-led units
Birth centres are homelike, run by midwives, and often have pools. For low-risk pregnancies they are safe for babies and have fewer interventions than labour wards.

## Hospital labour ward
Best if you or your baby need extra care. Doctors, epidurals and theatres are on hand.

## How to decide
Talk with your midwife about your health and what is near you. Visit your options if you can, and think about what helps you feel safe.

## When to call your midwife
- In labour, call your midwife or unit for any worry, wherever you plan to give birth

## Questions
Q: Can I change my mind about where to give birth?
A: Yes. You can change your plan at any time, including in labour.
Q: What if I need to transfer?
A: Your midwife will arrange it. Most transfers are not emergencies.
Q: Is home birth safe for a first baby?
A: There is a small extra risk for first babies. Talk it through with your midwife.

Evidence: Based on NICE intrapartum care guidance and the Birthplace in England study.
Sources: Birthplace in England study (2011); NICE guideline NG235: Intrapartum care; NHS: Where to give birth

---

# What to pack in your hospital bag
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/hospital-bag/
Stage: Birth

A packed bag takes one worry away. Mia gives you a short, calm list so you only bring what you need.

## In short
- For labour: Your birth plan and notes, comfortable clothes, snacks and drinks, a lip balm and a phone charger.
- For after: Loose clothes, comfy underwear, maternity pads, toiletries and a nursing bra if you plan to breastfeed.
- For baby: A few sleepsuits, vests, a hat, nappies and a car seat if you are driving home.
- When to pack: Many people pack by week 36. Keep the bag by the door.

## For labour
Your notes and birth plan. Loose, comfortable clothes or a nightie. Snacks, drinks and a water bottle with a straw. Lip balm, hair ties, a phone charger with a long cable, and something to help you relax, like music or a pillow.

## For after the birth
Loose clothes, big comfy knickers, plenty of maternity pads, nursing bras or vests, breast pads, toiletries, a towel and slippers.

## For your baby
A few sleepsuits and vests, a hat, socks, newborn nappies, cotton wool and a blanket. A car seat fitted in the car if you are driving home.

## For your birth partner
Snacks, a charger, a change of clothes, a toothbrush and change or a card for parking.

## When to pack
Many people pack by week 36. Keep the bag by the door, and make sure your partner knows where it is.

## When to call your midwife
- Packing is not urgent. For worries about labour, call your midwife

## Questions
Q: Do I need to bring my own pillow?
A: Many people like to. Check your unit’s advice.
Q: What should my birth partner bring?
A: Snacks, a charger, cash for parking and a change of clothes.
Q: How many nappies?
A: About 10 to 12 for a short stay.

Evidence: Based on NHS suggestions for what to pack for labour and birth.
Sources: NHS: Packing your bag for labour
