# Eating dates in late pregnancy: what the research says
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/dates-late-pregnancy/
Stage: Birth

Many people hear that eating dates near the end of pregnancy helps labour. Mia explains what the studies found and how strong the proof really is.

## In short
- What people do: Some people eat about six dates a day from week 36, as a snack.
- What studies found: Small studies suggest dates may help the cervix get ready and labour start on its own. The studies are small, so the proof is limited.
- Who should be careful: Dates are high in natural sugar. If you have gestational diabetes, ask your midwife or doctor first.
- Keep it simple: Dates are a food, not a treatment. They do not replace care from your midwife.

## Why people eat dates
Dates are a tradition in many cultures for the end of pregnancy. They are sweet, filling and full of fibre.

## What the studies found
A few small trials suggest that eating dates from week 36 may be linked with a readier cervix, a shorter early labour and less need for induction.
But the studies are small and not all agree, so the evidence is weak. More research is needed.

## How people eat them
Most studies used about six dates a day, around 60 to 80 grams, from week 36. Eat them as a snack, with yoghurt, or in porridge.

## Who should be careful
Dates are high in natural sugar. If you have gestational diabetes or another health condition, ask your midwife or doctor first.

## When to call your midwife
- Dates are a food, not a treatment. Call your midwife for any worries about labour

## Questions
Q: How many dates do people eat?
A: Studies often used about six dates a day, from week 36.
Q: Can dates start labour?
A: There is no proof they start labour. Some small studies link them with a readier cervix and less need for induction.
Q: Are dates safe in pregnancy?
A: Yes, as part of a balanced diet. Ask first if you have diabetes.

Evidence: Based on small clinical trials and reviews of date fruit in late pregnancy. The evidence is limited and more research is needed.
Sources: Small clinical trials and systematic reviews of date fruit in late pregnancy

---

# Perineal massage and tear prevention
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/perineal-tear-prevention/
Stage: Birth

Many people worry about tearing. Mia explains what the research says helps and how to talk about it with your midwife.

## In short
- Perineal massage: From about week 35, gentle daily massage may lower the chance of a serious tear in a first birth.
- In labour: A warm compress on the perineum while baby is crowning is linked with fewer serious tears.
- Positions: Upright, side-lying or all fours positions can lower strain. Ask your midwife what works for you.
- Healing: Keep clean and dry, rest, and use pain relief. Call if pain worsens or the wound smells.

## Tears are common
The perineum is the skin between your vagina and anus. Many people have a small tear or graze in a vaginal birth, especially with a first baby. Most heal well.
A smaller number have a deeper tear that involves the muscle around the back passage. These need repair in theatre and extra care afterwards.

## Perineal massage
From about week 34 to 35, gentle massage of the perineum a few times a week may lower the chance of tears that need stitches and of an episiotomy, especially in a first birth.
Use clean hands and a plain oil. Press gently down and to the sides for a few minutes. Your partner can help.

## In labour
A warm compress held on the perineum as your baby crowns is linked with fewer serious tears.
Slow, controlled pushing as the head is born, guided by your midwife, also helps.

## Positions
Upright, side-lying or all-fours positions may help. Talk to your midwife about what suits you.

## After a tear
Keep the area clean and dry, change pads often, and pour warm water over it when you pee. Rest, take pain relief and drink plenty.
Pelvic floor exercises help healing. Ask for a referral to a physio if needed.

## When to call your midwife
- Pain that gets worse
- The wound smells bad or has pus
- Fever
- You cannot control wind or poo

## Questions
Q: Does everybody tear?
A: No. Many people have no tear, or a small one that heals easily.
Q: Is an episiotomy common?
A: It is used only when needed. Talk to your midwife about when it might be offered.
Q: When can I start massage?
A: Usually from around week 34 to 35.

Evidence: Based on Cochrane review of perineal massage and RCOG guidance on tears.
Sources: Cochrane review: Antenatal perineal massage; RCOG: Perineal tears during childbirth; Cochrane review: Perineal techniques during the second stage of labour

---

# Pain relief options in labour
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/pain-relief-in-labour/
Stage: Birth

There is no right or wrong way to cope with labour. Here is every option, fairly, so you can choose and change your mind.

## In short
- Without medicine: Warm water, massage, movement, breathing and a calm room can all help.
- TENS and gas and air: TENS is a small machine with pads on your back. Gas and air works fast and wears off quickly.
- Injections: Pethidine or similar can take the edge off pain but may make you or baby drowsy.
- Epidural: This gives the strongest relief. It means staying on the bed and may make pushing or the later stage of labour longer.

## Your options
There are many ways to cope with labour pain. You can use one or several, and you can change your mind at any time.

## Without drugs
Water, massage, movement, breathing, hypnobirthing and a calm room all help. Continuous support from someone you trust is one of the best ways to cope.

## TENS
A small machine with sticky pads on your back sends tiny electrical pulses. It may help in early labour. It cannot be used in water.

## Gas and air
Entonox is breathed in through a mouthpiece. It works fast and wears off quickly. It may make you feel light-headed or sick.

## Opioid injections
Pethidine or diamorphine can help you relax and cope. They may make you drowsy or sick, and can affect your baby’s breathing and early feeding if given close to birth.

## Epidural
An epidural numbs the lower body and gives the best pain relief. It means staying in bed with monitoring and a drip.
It can make the pushing stage longer and slightly raise the chance of an assisted birth. It does not raise the chance of a caesarean.

## When to call your midwife
- Ask your midwife about pain relief at any point in labour

## Questions
Q: Can I change my mind about pain relief?
A: Yes, at any time. It is your choice.
Q: Does an epidural harm my baby?
A: It is generally considered safe. Your anaesthetist can talk through the risks with you.
Q: Is an epidural always available?
A: Only in hospital labour wards, not at home or in most birth centres.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE guidance on pain relief in labour.
Sources: NHS: Pain relief in labour; NICE guideline NG235: Intrapartum care; Cochrane review: Epidural versus non-epidural analgesia

---

# Induction of labour: what to expect
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/induction-of-labour/
Stage: Birth

Induction means starting labour with medical help. Here is why it is offered, how it works and the questions worth asking.

## In short
- Why it is offered: Common reasons are going past your due date, your waters breaking without labour, or a health concern for you or baby.
- How it works: It can start with a gel or pessary, a balloon, a membrane sweep or a hormone drip, step by step.
- It can take time: Induction often takes longer than labour that starts on its own. Bring things to pass the time.
- Ask questions: Ask what the risks are of both inducing and waiting, and what your other choices are.

## Why induction is offered
Induction means starting labour artificially. It is offered when waiting longer may be riskier for you or your baby than starting labour now.
Common reasons are going past 41 weeks, your waters breaking without labour starting, or health concerns like high blood pressure or diabetes.

## How it works
It often starts with a membrane sweep. Then a pessary or gel to soften the cervix, or a small balloon.
Next, your waters may be broken, and a hormone drip (oxytocin) may be used to start contractions.

## How long it takes
Induction can take a day or more, especially with a first baby. Bring things to pass the time and snacks.

## What to ask
Ask: why is it advised for me? What are the risks of waiting? What are the options, and can I go home during the early part?

## When to call your midwife
- Waters break, bleeding, or your baby moves less while you wait

## Questions
Q: Can I say no to induction?
A: Yes. It is your decision. Your team will explain the risks and benefits so you can choose.
Q: Does a membrane sweep hurt?
A: It can feel uncomfortable or crampy for a short time.
Q: Is induction more painful?
A: Contractions can feel stronger, and more people ask for an epidural.

Evidence: Based on NICE guideline on inducing labour and NHS guidance.
Sources: NICE guideline NG207: Inducing labour; NHS: Inducing labour

---

# Caesarean birth: planned and unplanned
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/caesarean-birth/
Stage: Birth

A caesarean is a real birth. Here is why it may be advised, what happens, and how you can still make it feel like yours.

## In short
- Why it happens: Reasons include baby’s position, a health concern or labour not progressing. Some are planned and some are not.
- What happens: You are usually awake with a spinal block. The operation is quick, and your birth partner can often be there.
- Make it yours: Ask about skin-to-skin in theatre, delayed cord clamping and your feeding plan.
- Recovery: Rest, gentle walking and pain relief help. Call your midwife about a fever, a wound that looks red or smells, or heavy bleeding.

## Why a caesarean happens
A caesarean is an operation to deliver your baby through a cut in your tummy and womb. About four in ten births in England are now caesareans.
It can be planned, for example for a breech baby or placenta problems, or happen in labour if needed. You can also ask for one.

## What happens
You are usually awake with a spinal or epidural, so you feel no pain, only pulling. A screen hides the operation, and your birth partner can sit by your head.
Your baby is born in about 10 minutes. The full operation takes around 40 minutes.

## Making it yours
Ask for skin-to-skin in theatre, delayed cord clamping, a lowered screen to see your baby born, and your own music.

## Recovery
Expect to stay in hospital one to two days. Walking soon after helps healing.
Avoid heavy lifting for about six weeks. Ask before driving.

## Future births
Many people can have a vaginal birth after a caesarean (VBAC). About three in four who try succeed.

## When to call your midwife
- Wound red, hot, leaking or smelly
- Fever
- Heavy bleeding
- Pain or swelling in one leg
- Breathlessness or chest pain. Call 999

## Questions
Q: Can I have skin-to-skin after a caesarean?
A: Often, yes. Ask your team before the birth.
Q: Can I have a vaginal birth after a caesarean?
A: Many people can. Talk to your midwife or doctor early in pregnancy.
Q: How long is recovery?
A: Around six weeks for most people.

Evidence: Based on NICE caesarean birth guideline and NHS guidance.
Sources: NICE guideline NG192: Caesarean birth; NHS: Caesarean section; RCOG: Birth after previous caesarean

---

# The first six weeks after birth
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/after-birth/
Stage: After birth

The first weeks after birth are a big change. Take them one day at a time: the golden hour, feeding, healing and how you are feeling.

## In short
- The golden hour: Skin-to-skin right after birth helps your baby stay warm and calm, and can help feeding start.
- Feeding: Breast, bottle or both. Mia explains each and when to ask for help.
- Healing: Bleeding, stitches and tiredness are normal. Know the signs that need a call to your midwife.
- Your mood: Feeling low for a few days is common. If it lasts more than two weeks, talk to someone.

## The first hour
Skin-to-skin right after birth keeps your baby warm, calms their breathing and heartbeat, and helps feeding start. It is good for you too.
Routine checks can usually wait until after this first hour.

## The first days
Your midwife will check you and your baby, often at home. Your baby will be offered a physical exam and a heel-prick test around day five.
Bleeding is heaviest in the first days. Rest as much as you can, and let others look after you.

## Feeding
Breast milk, formula or both can all nourish your baby. Feeding often in the first weeks is normal.
Ask for help early if feeding hurts or your baby is not feeding well.

## Your body
Bleeding (lochia) can last up to six weeks. Stitches, after-pains and sore breasts are common.
Pelvic floor exercises help you recover. Your six-week check with your GP is a chance to talk about how you feel.

## Your mood
Many people feel teary and low around days three to five. These baby blues usually pass within two weeks.
If low mood or anxiety lasts longer, talk to your midwife, health visitor or GP. You are not alone.

## When to call your midwife
- Heavy bleeding, or passing large clots
- Fever, or feeling hot and shivery
- Pain or swelling in one leg
- A bad headache, or problems with your eyes
- Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Call 999 or your GP now
- Your baby is floppy, very sleepy, not feeding, or has yellow skin in the first day

## Questions
Q: When should I get help for my mood?
A: If you feel low for more than two weeks, or have scary thoughts, call your midwife or doctor now.
Q: Is skin-to-skin possible after a caesarean?
A: Often, yes. Ask your team about it before the birth.
Q: When does bleeding stop?
A: Usually within six weeks. It should get lighter and change colour over time.

Evidence: Based on WHO recommendations on postnatal care and NHS guidance after birth.
Sources: WHO recommendations on maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience; NICE guideline NG194: Postnatal care; NHS: Your body after the birth

---

# Delayed cord clamping and the golden hour
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/delayed-cord-clamping/
Stage: After birth

What happens in the first minutes after birth matters. Mia explains cord clamping and the golden hour in plain words.

## In short
- Waiting helps: Waiting at least one minute before clamping lets more blood pass to baby and is advised for most births.
- Skin-to-skin: Holding baby on your chest keeps them warm and calm and helps feeding start.
- The golden hour: Try to keep the first hour calm and uninterrupted. Routine checks can often wait.
- If baby needs help: Sometimes the cord is cut sooner so baby can get care. Your team will tell you why.

## What delayed cord clamping is
After your baby is born, the cord still carries blood from the placenta to your baby. Waiting before clamping lets more of this blood reach your baby.

## Why it helps
Waiting at least a minute is linked with better iron levels in babies in the first months.
For premature babies, it is linked with better outcomes too. NICE and WHO both advise waiting for most healthy babies.

## The golden hour
The first hour after birth is a special time. Skin-to-skin helps your baby stay warm and calm, and helps feeding start.
Ask for the room to stay calm and quiet, and for checks to wait unless needed.

## If things are different
If your baby needs help breathing, the cord may be cut sooner. Many units can now help babies with the cord still attached.
After a caesarean, delayed clamping and skin-to-skin are often still possible.

## When to call your midwife
- Your midwife will look after you both in the first hour. Speak up if you have any worries

## Questions
Q: Can I do this after a caesarean?
A: Often, yes. Ask your team about it before the birth.
Q: Does waiting raise any risk?
A: For healthy babies, waiting at least a minute is recommended. Your team will advise if there is a concern.
Q: Can my partner cut the cord?
A: Often, yes. Add it to your birth plan.

Evidence: Based on WHO and NICE guidance on cord clamping and immediate skin-to-skin contact.
Sources: NICE guideline NG235: Intrapartum care; WHO: Optimal timing of cord clamping; Cochrane review: Effect of timing of umbilical cord clamping

---

# Breastfeeding basics for new parents
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/breastfeeding-basics/
Stage: After birth

Feeding is a skill you and your baby learn together. Here are the basics, and where to find help, whatever you choose.

## In short
- The first feed: Skin-to-skin soon after birth helps baby find the breast. Ask for help with the first feed.
- A good latch: Baby’s mouth wide open, chin touching the breast, and feeding should not hurt after the first few seconds.
- How often: Newborns feed often, about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. Feed when baby shows early hunger signs.
- Ask for help: Pain, a baby who is not feeding or not having wet nappies need a call to your midwife or feeding specialist.

## Getting started
Skin-to-skin soon after birth helps your baby find the breast. The first milk, colostrum, is thick, yellow and full of goodness, even in small amounts.
Your milk usually comes in around day two to four.

## A good latch
Hold your baby close, nose to nipple. Wait for a wide-open mouth, then bring them to the breast, chin first.
A good latch should not hurt after the first few seconds. You will hear swallowing.

## How often
Newborns feed often, 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, including at night. Feed when your baby shows early signs, like rooting or sucking hands.
By day five, expect at least six wet nappies a day.

## Common problems
Sore nipples, engorged breasts and blocked ducts are common. Most can be fixed with help with the latch.
If a breast is red, hot and painful and you feel unwell, it may be mastitis. Call your GP.

## Where to get help
Your midwife, health visitor, a breastfeeding counsellor or the National Breastfeeding Helpline can help.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby has fewer wet nappies than expected, or seems very sleepy and not feeding
- Your baby’s skin or eyes look yellow
- A red, hot, painful area on your breast, with fever
- Bleeding or cracked nipples that are not getting better

## Questions
Q: What if I choose to bottle feed?
A: That is a valid choice. Mia explains bottle feeding safely too.
Q: Is it normal for feeding to hurt at first?
A: A little tenderness can be common. Ongoing pain is not, so ask for help with the latch.
Q: How do I know my baby is getting enough?
A: Wet and dirty nappies, steady weight gain and a content baby are good signs.

Evidence: Based on WHO and NHS guidance on breastfeeding and the UNICEF Baby Friendly Initiative.
Sources: NHS: Breastfeeding; UNICEF UK Baby Friendly Initiative; WHO: Breastfeeding recommendations

---

# Safe sleep for newborns
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/newborn-safe-sleep/
Stage: After birth

Safe sleep is simple once you know it. Mia gives you the short list so you can rest more easily.

## In short
- On the back: Always put baby to sleep on their back, for every sleep.
- Own space: A firm, flat mattress in a cot or Moses basket in your room for the first six months.
- Keep it clear: No pillows, bumpers, loose blankets or soft toys in the sleep space.
- Avoid risk: Do not sleep with baby on a sofa or armchair, and do not smoke around baby.

## Back to sleep
Always put your baby on their back to sleep, for every sleep, day and night. This is the most important thing you can do to lower the risk of sudden infant death.

## A clear, flat space
Use a firm, flat, waterproof mattress in a cot or Moses basket. No pillows, duvets, bumpers or soft toys.
Place your baby with their feet at the foot of the cot, so they cannot wriggle under covers.

## Same room
Keep your baby in a cot in your room for at least the first six months.

## The right temperature
A room temperature of 16 to 20 degrees is ideal. Do not use hats indoors, and check your baby’s chest or back to see if they are too hot.

## Things to avoid
Never sleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair. Do not smoke during pregnancy or around your baby.
If you share a bed, do it safely. Do not share if you or your partner smoke, have drunk alcohol, or taken drugs or sedating medicines.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby is floppy, hard to wake or has trouble breathing. Call 999
- Your baby has a fever or is unusually sleepy

## Questions
Q: Is it safe to share a bed?
A: The safest place is a separate cot in your room. Read the risks, especially if you smoke, drink or take sedating medicine.
Q: How warm should the room be?
A: Between 16 and 20 degrees is advised. Dress baby lightly.
Q: Can my baby sleep in a sling or car seat?
A: Not for long periods. Move them to a flat surface for sleep.

Evidence: Based on NHS and The Lullaby Trust guidance on safer sleep.
Sources: The Lullaby Trust: Safer sleep advice; NHS: Reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome

---

# Postnatal recovery: body and mind
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/postnatal-recovery/
Stage: After birth

Your body has done something huge. Give yourself time to rest and heal, and know the signs that need a call.

## In short
- Bleeding: Bleeding for a few weeks is normal. Call if it is very heavy, smells bad or you pass large clots.
- Stitches and soreness: Keep clean and dry, rest, and use pain relief as advised. Call if pain gets worse.
- Pelvic floor: Gentle pelvic floor exercises can start soon after birth. Ask your midwife or physio.
- Rest and mood: Sleep when you can and accept help. Low mood that lasts more than two weeks needs a talk with your doctor.

## Bleeding
Bleeding, called lochia, starts heavy and red and gets lighter and browner over a few weeks. It can last up to six weeks.
Use maternity pads, not tampons.

## Stitches and soreness
Keep the area clean and dry. Pour warm water over it when you pee, and change pads often.
Pain relief, rest and a cool pad can help. Stitches usually dissolve in a few weeks.

## After a caesarean
Keep the wound clean and dry. Wear loose clothes and avoid heavy lifting for about six weeks.

## Pelvic floor
Start gentle pelvic floor exercises in the first days. Some leaking is common at first, but tell your GP if it does not get better.
A pelvic health physio can help a lot.

## Rest, food and help
Sleep when your baby sleeps, eat well and drink plenty, especially if breastfeeding. Accept help from family and friends.

## Your six-week check
Your GP will check how you are healing, your mood and contraception. Bring any questions.

## When to call your midwife
- Heavy bleeding, or passing large clots
- Bleeding that smells bad
- Fever or feeling unwell
- Pain or swelling in one leg
- Chest pain or breathlessness. Call 999

## Questions
Q: When can I exercise again?
A: Gentle walking is fine early on. Ask your midwife or doctor before harder exercise, often after the 6 week check.
Q: When is the 6 week check?
A: Usually between 6 and 8 weeks after birth. Your GP will check you.
Q: When can I have sex again?
A: When you feel ready. You can get pregnant again soon after birth, so think about contraception.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE postnatal care guidance.
Sources: NICE guideline NG194: Postnatal care; NHS: Your body after the birth; Pelvic, Obstetric and Gynaecological Physiotherapy (POGP)

---

# Postnatal depression: signs and where to get help
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/postnatal-depression/
Stage: After birth

Many new parents feel low. Mia explains the difference between baby blues and depression and how to get help fast.

## In short
- Baby blues: Tearfulness and mood swings in the first two weeks are common and pass.
- Postnatal depression: If low mood, anxiety or feeling unable to cope lasts more than two weeks, speak to your midwife, health visitor or GP.
- Partners too: Partners can also feel low. Help is for them as well.
- Urgent help: If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, call your GP, 111 or 999 now.

## Baby blues
In the first two weeks, many parents feel teary, anxious or irritable. This is called the baby blues and usually passes on its own.

## Postnatal depression
About one in ten new mothers have postnatal depression. It can start any time in the first year.
Signs include low mood most days, losing interest in things, trouble bonding, feeling hopeless, and anxiety.

## Anxiety and other conditions
Postnatal anxiety, OCD and post-traumatic stress after a difficult birth are common too. Rarely, a serious illness called postpartum psychosis can start suddenly in the first weeks. It is an emergency.

## Getting help
Talk to your midwife, health visitor or GP. Talking therapies and medicine can help, and many are safe with breastfeeding.
Partners can get postnatal depression too, and help is there for them as well.

## When to call your midwife
- Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Call 999 or go to A&E
- Hearing or seeing things others do not, or very confused thinking. Call 999
- Low mood that lasts more than two weeks. Talk to your GP

## Questions
Q: Is it my fault?
A: No. It is an illness, not a failure, and it is treatable.
Q: Will treatment affect breastfeeding?
A: Some treatments are fine while breastfeeding. Your doctor can advise.
Q: Can partners get it?
A: Yes. Help is there for partners too.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE guidance on perinatal mental health.
Sources: NHS: Postnatal depression; NICE guideline CG192: Antenatal and postnatal mental health; Mind: Perinatal mental health
